Growing access to shared power and water treatment is shifting some of the capital burden of African textile production from manufacturers to industrial park developers. In some of the continent's textile hubs, developers are providing common utilities that textile producers pay to use, reducing the installations each factory needs to finance. Already, wastewater plants are operating in industrial zones in Ethiopia, Benin and Togo, alongside factory sites, grid connections and logistics services. stories.title: Liberia: 'The State Will Either Prosecute or Release'
stories.summary: Liberia: 'The State Will Either Prosecute or Release' 29 October 2026 Liberian Observer (Monrovia) By David a. Lamin-Blamo, nominee for Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Liberia, has pledged to review pretrial detention cases nationwide, strengthen criminal prosecutions and pursue corruption and drug trafficking cases, disclosing that 2,848 of the 4,125 persons held in the country's prisons as of September 2026 had never been tried. Appearing before the Liberian Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions, Lamin-Blamo said the high number of pretrial detainees, many of whom cannot afford legal representation or bond, reflects serious challenges within the country's criminal justice system. She disclosed that Monrovia Central Prison alone holds 1,888 inmates, including 1,312 pretrial detainees, representing more than 69 percent of the prison's population. "These figures fall hardest on the poor, who cannot afford a lawyer or a bond," she told senators, promising that, if confirmed, she would extend an ongoing review of pretrial detention cases at Monrovia Central Prison to correctional facilities across Liberia. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "The State will either prosecute or release in accordance with law," she declared.

stories.title: Liberia: Boakai Announces U.S.$30m Geological Survey, Gold Refinery Plan
stories.summary: Liberia: Boakai Announces U.S.$30m Geological Survey, Gold Refinery Plan 29 October 2026 Liberian Observer (Monrovia) By David a. Yates President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. has announced plans for a US$30 million geological survey to identify Liberia's mineral potential, alongside a commitment to establish the country's first gold-processing facility within two years as his administration seeks to attract investment and increase national benefits from the mining sector. Boakai said the planned airborne geophysical data collection, to be undertaken under the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) compact, would strengthen Liberia's geological information, particularly on critical and strategic minerals, and provide investors with better information for exploration and development decisions. Delivering the keynote address at the opening of the second Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Exhibition (LIMEC 2026) at the Farmington Hotel in Harbel, Margibi County, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, the President said Liberia must improve its understanding of its mineral resources while creating the conditions necessary for responsible investment and local value addition. He said the government intends to use the geological survey to support a coordinated national exploration programme over the next five years, improve access to reliable mineral data, and strengthen the country's position in attracting credible mining companies.

stories.summary: Tanzania: Study Warns Rising Drug-Resistant Infections Among Newborns 29 October 2026 Tanzania Daily News (Dar es Salaam) By Nashon Kennedy Mwanza — NEWBORNS face a growing threat from severe infections that are increasingly difficult to treat because of bacteria resistant to multiple antibiotics, a study conducted at Bugando Medical Centre (BMC) has revealed. Presenting her findings in Mwanza, Dr Delfina Msanga of the Catholic University of Health and Allied Sciences said neonatal sepsis remained a major concern because newborns have immature immune systems and infections can become life-threatening rapidly. Her research, titled "Gut Bacterial Microbiome Diversity and Multi Drug Resistant Neonatal Sepsis Among Neonates Admitted at Bugando Medical Centre in Mwanza, Tanzania," highlights the need for improved diagnosis, infection prevention and responsible antibiotic use. A review of 12 hospitalbased studies in Tanzania found a pooled prevalence of microbiologically confirmed neonatal sepsis of 33 per cent, while the pooled case-fatality rate was 16 per cent. La province désertique et montagneuse du Tibesti, frontalière de la Libye et du Niger, est en proie à de vives tensions liées à l’exploitation d’importantes réserves d’or (illustration). © MICHAEL RUNKEL / ROBERT HARDING RF / ROBERTHARDING VIA AFP Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 09h55 Lecture : 2 minutes. Brigade minière vs Comité d’autodéfense de Miski Le 14 octobre, deux membres de la Brigade minière, des forces de sécurité dépendantes du ministère des Mines, ont été tués et neuf autres blessés dans une attaque perpétrée par le Comité d’autodéfense de Miski. la suite après cette publicité Le Comité d’autodéfense accuse la Brigade minière d’avoir « introduit des activités d’exploitation aurifère et des prélèvements auprès des orpailleurs, en contradiction » avec l’accord de paix signé en 2025 avec les autorités tchadiennes. « Le Comité déplore toute perte de vie humaine, quel que soit le camp, et demande la démilitarisation de la zone de Miski ainsi que la reprise du dialogue afin de garantir le respect et l’application de l’accord de paix », assure son porte-parole.

"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict. Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training. The two-day Russia-Africa Summit, the third since 2019, comes as Moscow grapples with heavy sanctions over its Ukraine offensive - and as several African governments turn to it for security assistance. A total of 48 African countries have sent delegations to the summit, including 22 heads of state, with Russian President Vladimir Putin planning to meet most of them one-on-one. Africa plays a central role in Russia's strategy to establish itself as the leader of the Global South, said Cécile Marin, a specialist in Russian-African relations and a lecturer at Sciences Po Paris. "Russia is putting forward a whole narrative denouncing the neocolonialism of the Western powers. Obviously, France is a major target," she told RFI.

stories.summary: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 29, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 29 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda One Year After Tanzania's Election Crackdown, Victims' Families Demand Justice One year after deadly election-related violence in Tanzania that left at least 518 people dead, families of victims are demanding justice, accountability and financial assistance for medical treatment. stories.title: Sudan: Sudan Once Again Accuses Ethiopia of Involvement in Drone Strikes Targeting Power Stations, Civilian Sites
stories.summary: Sudan Once Again Accuses Ethiopia of Involvement in Drone Strikes Targeting Power Stations, Civilian Sites 29 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Sudan has once again accused neighbouring Ethiopia of involvement in drone attacks targeting civilian infrastructure, fuel depots and power stations, alleging that drones used in recent strikes were launched from Ethiopian territory, including Bahir Dar Airport. According to Sudan Tribune , Sudanese government and intelligence officials made the allegations at a joint press conference in Khartoum on Wednesday, presenting what they described as flight data, satellite imagery and fragments of intercepted drones to support their claims. The accusations followed a series of strikes on Sudanese infrastructure. On Tuesday, a drone attack disabled the Markhiyat power station northwest of Omdurman, disrupting electricity supplies across the capital area. Further strikes on Wednesday targeted a power station and fuel storage facilities in El Manaqil, Gezira State, as well as fuel storage sites and a pipeline linked to Bashayer Port in Red Sea State.

stories.title: Tanzania: No Accountability One Year After Tanzania Election Violence
stories.summary: Tanzania: No Accountability One Year After Tanzania Election Violence file photo - AI generated Tanzaniaâs disputed October 29 elections were followed by mass protests and mass protests. 28 October 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) By Oryem Nyeko Families of People Killed, Missing Await Justice One year after Tanzania's contested 2025 elections, authorities have yet to make any arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the vote. In the months leading up to the elections, the government intensified its repression of the political opposition, government critics, and the media. Authorities also failed to account for a spate of apparent enforced disappearances, including that of former Tanzanian ambassador to Cuba Humphrey Polepole , who was reported missing just weeks before the elections. Polepole had publicly criticized the ruling party, Chama Cha Mapinduzi, for not being "aligned with safeguarding human rights, peace, and respect for people." His whereabouts remain unknown. Matshe said the central bank and Treasury would only advance towards a single-currency system when economic conditions support the transition, with eight publicly announced preconditions guiding the process. stories.title: Liberia: Liberia Begins Countdown to UN Security Council Presidency
stories.summary: Liberia Begins Countdown to UN Security Council Presidency 29 October 2026 Liberian Observer (Monrovia) The Government of Liberia has officially launched its "Road to the United Nations Security Council Presidency," beginning a series of national and diplomatic engagements ahead of the country's historic assumption of the Council's rotating presidency in December 2026. The launch took place Monday, October 26, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Monrovia during the commemoration of United Nations Day, held under the theme, "Liberia on the United Nations Security Council: From Sustaining Peace at Home to Advancing Peace and Security Globally." The initiative marks a significant moment in Liberia's diplomatic history, as the country prepares to preside over the 15-member Security Council for the first time since its earlier membership in 1961. Liberia was elected in June 2025 to serve as a non-permanent member for the 2026-2027 term, securing 181 votes in the United Nations General Assembly. Delivering special remarks, Foreign Affairs Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti described Liberia's return to a leadership position at the United Nations as the outcome of decades of diplomatic engagement, national resilience and contributions by successive administrations. stories.title: Africa: Unitaid Extends Investment in Hepatitis C Prevention for People Who Inject Drugs
stories.summary: Africa: Unitaid Extends Investment in Hepatitis C Prevention for People Who Inject Drugs Nick Youngson/Picpedia Hepatitis C 28 October 2026 UNITAID (Geneva) Hepatitis C is curable. But every year, nearly one million people still acquire the infection. People who inject drugs are among those most affected, often without access to the equipment and services that could help prevent it. As a major funder in the fight against hepatitis C, Unitaid is supporting the global elimination targets through prevention, testing and treatment, focusing on the most marginalized and vulnerable populations. Building on this broader work, Unitaid is now reaffirming its commitment to hepatitis C prevention and harm reduction through investing an additional US$7.8 million in three projects expanding hepatitis C prevention and care for people who inject drugs in ten low- and middle-income countries.

stories.title: Africa: Ending Conflict Is 'Number One Thing' to Reduce World Hunger, New WFP Chief Says
stories.summary: Africa: Ending Conflict Is 'Number One Thing' to Reduce World Hunger, New WFP Chief Says Hedley Tah/WFP Loading finished, the cargo plane is ready for take-off - bound for South Sudan's conflict-hit Jonglei State. 28 October 2026 UN News Service Reducing conflict is the single most effective way to tackle global hunger, the new head of the UN World Food Programme (WFP), Luke Lindberg , said on Wednesday, noting that conflict drives two thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide. " Conflict is a man-made situation. It is something that we can solve ," Mr. Lindberg told journalists at UN Headquarters in New York in his first press conference since taking office earlier this week. "The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict that is happening all around the world." On top of that, El Niño is set to push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity, while chokepoints in global supply chains are exacerbating the problem further, he said. stories.title: Sudan: Civilians in Sudan's El Obeid Trapped Between Drones and Incarceration
stories.summary: Sudan: Civilians in Sudan's El Obeid Trapped Between Drones and Incarceration Ante Bussmann/MSF Entrance to Nyala Teaching Hospital, South Darfur. Sudan, May 2026. 28 October 2026 UN News Service Civilians in Sudan's El Obeid live in constant fear of drone attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and of a wave of arbitrary arrests by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), UN-appointed independent investigators said on Wednesday. They warned that the war is becoming more geographically extensive, technologically sophisticated and increasingly dangerous for civilians. " Thousands have been arrested by SAF security cells, detained and tortured in unofficial locations and in El Obeid Central Prison, kept under appalling conditions ," said Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan , during a press briefing. "These practices must stop immediately." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The Mission released its new report , Sudan's Unrelenting War: Civilian Devastation and Deepening Insecurity in El Obeid, after presenting its September findings on external support for the warring parties to the General Assembly's Third Committee. Drones and detention The report found that RSF drone strikes continue to kill and injure civilians in El Obeid, damaging homes, schools, displacement sites and electricity and water systems, and may amount to war crimes. Only around 30 per cent of hospitals in the city remained operational after attacks, one expert told the Mission.

stories.title: Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
stories.summary: Image caption, Neema Munuo, whose 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami was shot dead on the day of the election, wants the government to acknowledge her suffering By Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Dar es Salaam ,Â Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Lucy Fleming Published 29 October 2026, 00:25 GMT Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured. "We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC. On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear". The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded. Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing. He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.

stories.title: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Marry Mubaiwa in an image from 2018 when she was still married to Constantino Chiwenga By Patrick Jackson Published 27 October 2026 The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder. Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa. Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said. The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses. Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.

stories.title: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola By Basillioh Rukanga Reporting from Nairobi Published 21 October 2026 Updated 27 October 2026 As fears grow that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could spread further, Kenya, which announced its first Ebola case three weeks ago and has since had eight more cases, is hoping for the opposite. Nine cases and two deaths have so far been confirmed. With the first 20 of the people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient being released, the government has described it as a "milestone worth celebrating". The government expects the outbreak to be declared over in less than two months, if efforts to contain the spread holds. But that is assuming there are no more cases, including from the 98 people still in quarantine and due to be freed next week.

stories.title: Controversial Islamic cleric shot dead in northern Nigeria
stories.summary: Image source, Massussuka Media Image caption, Yahaya Masussuka was awarded a peace prize last year by Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 27 October 2026 A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina. Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC. The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said. It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death. It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels.

stories.title: Paddy Donnelly obituary
stories.summary: Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa View image in fullscreen Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa Obituary Paddy Donnelly obituary My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity. In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive. He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.
